title: Unit 4g - C++ References Title Slide
summary: Title slide introducing Unit 4g on C++ References in CS103, taught by Mark Redekopp. Covers how references work as aliases in C++.
main_text: This unit covers C++ References, a feature in C++ that allows creating aliases (alternate names) for existing variables. The unit is part of CS103 and is taught by Mark Redekopp. Topics include the difference between pointers and references, how to declare and use C++ reference variables, pass-by-reference using C++ references, const references, and proper usage patterns.
notes_text: This is the introductory slide for Unit 4g. Students should already be familiar with pointers from earlier units, as this unit builds on that knowledge by introducing C++ references as a simpler alternative syntax for pass-by-reference.

title: Review of Pointer to an Int
summary: Reviews declaring an integer pointer using int* syntax. Shows how z stores the address of y and points to its memory location.
main_text: Given the declaration 'int y=3;', the question asks what is being declared with 'int* z = &y;'. The answer is: a pointer to an int. The variable z is a pointer variable that holds the address of y. In the memory diagram, y is stored at address 1a0 with value 3, and z is stored at address 1a8 containing the value 1a0 (the address of y). The arrow from z to y indicates that z points to y. This is a review of pointer fundamentals before introducing C++ references.
notes_text: This review establishes the baseline understanding of pointers. The key concept is that int* creates a new variable that occupies memory and stores an address. This contrasts with C++ references introduced later, which do not create a new variable.

images.description: Memory diagram showing variable y at address 1a0 holding value 3, and pointer z at address 1a8 holding value 1a0, with an arrow from z to y indicating the pointer relationship

title: Review of Pointer to a Vector
summary: Reviews declaring a pointer to a vector of ints. Shows how vp stores the address of vector v1 and its internal memory layout.
main_text: Given 'vector<int> v1;', the question asks what is declared with 'vector<int>* vp = &v1;'. The answer is: a pointer to a vector of ints. The vector v1 is shown at address 2c0 with internal fields: a data pointer, capacity of 10, and size of 6. The underlying array contains values [50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 10] with additional uninitialized capacity slots shown as '?'. The pointer vp at address 2e0 stores the value 2c0, pointing to v1. This demonstrates that pointers work with any type, including complex objects like vectors.
notes_text: Understanding vector internal structure (data pointer, capacity, size) is important for understanding why passing vectors by value is expensive (deep copy) and why pass-by-reference is preferred for large objects.

images.description: Memory diagram showing vector v1 at address 2c0 with internal data pointer, capacity 10, size 6, and underlying array with values 50-54 and 10 plus uninitialized slots. Pointer vp at 2e0 stores 2c0.

title: Review of Pointer to a Quad Object
summary: Reviews declaring a pointer to a custom Quad object. Shows how qp stores the address of q1 with its internal pts_ and valid arrays.
main_text: Given 'Quad q1;', the question asks what is declared with 'Quad* qp = &q1;'. The answer is: a pointer to a Quad. The Quad object q1 is stored at address 4d0 and contains two data members: pts_ (a 2x4 array with values like 0,2,2,0 and 0,0,2,2) and valid (a boolean array with all T values). The pointer qp is stored at address 4f8 and contains the value 4d0, pointing to q1. This demonstrates that pointers can reference user-defined class objects.
notes_text: The Quad class appears to store four 2D points (forming a quadrilateral) with x-coordinates in one row and y-coordinates in another, plus validity flags. This example reinforces that pointer syntax works uniformly for any type.

images.description: Memory diagram showing Quad object q1 at address 4d0 with pts_ 2D array and valid boolean array, and pointer qp at 4f8 storing address 4d0

title: Review of Pointer Syntax and Address-Of Operator
summary: Summarizes pointer declaration syntax T* and the address-of operator & used in expressions. Pointers create a new variable that stores addresses.
main_text: Given a T variable/object declared as 'T varname;', declaring a T* creates a (small) new variable that can hold an address of ANY T object. The syntax is 'T* ptrname;'. Using & in an expression (right side of assignment) yields the 'address of' the variable: 'ptrname = &varname;'. Key emphasis: declaring a pointer creates a new variable in memory. The & operator extracts the memory address of an existing variable and stores it in the pointer. The slide uses a suitcase metaphor with a tag to represent the pointer-variable relationship.
notes_text: The highlighted phrases 'creates a (small) new variable' and 'address of' are critical distinctions that will contrast with C++ references in the next slides. Pointers allocate memory; references do not.

images.description: Visual metaphor showing a suitcase representing a T object at address 0x2f0, with a luggage tag representing a T* pointer that stores the address 0x2f0

title: C++ Reference Introduction - Alias Concept
summary: Introduces C++ references using int& syntax. A reference allocates no memory and simply creates an alias (another name) for an existing variable.
main_text: Given 'int y=3;', the declaration 'int& z = y;' creates a 'reference' (alias) to an int. A C++ Reference Type (T&) ALLOCATES NO MEMORY; it associates another name (an alias) to an already-alive variable. In the memory diagram, both y and z refer to the same memory location at address 1a0 containing value 3. There is no separate memory box for z -- it is shown as a second label on the same memory cell. A crossed-out icon emphasizes that no new memory is created. This is the fundamental difference between pointers and references.
notes_text: This is one of the most important slides in the unit. The key takeaway is that int& does NOT create a new variable. It simply gives another name to an existing variable. The crossed-out memory icon reinforces that no allocation occurs, unlike pointer declarations which do allocate space.

images.description: Memory diagram showing a single memory cell at address 1a0 with value 3, labeled with both y and z as names. A crossed-out icon indicates no new memory is allocated for z.

title: C++ Reference Aliasing Behavior
summary: Demonstrates that assigning to a reference variable modifies the original variable. Setting z=4 updates y to 4 because z is just another name for y.
main_text: Given 'int y=3;' and 'int& z = y;', the question asks what happens when 'z = 4;' is executed. The answer: y is updated to 4. Since z is y (just another name for the same memory location), assigning to z directly modifies y. The memory diagram shows the value at address 1a0 changing from 3 (crossed out) to 4, with both labels y and z still pointing to that same cell. The key insight is that 'z is y' -- they are the same variable with two names.
notes_text: This slide demonstrates the practical consequence of aliasing. Students must understand that any operation on z is literally an operation on y. There is no indirection or dereferencing needed, unlike with pointers where you would need *ptr to modify the pointed-to value.

images.description: Memory diagram at address 1a0 showing value 3 crossed out and replaced with 4, with both y and z labels on the same cell

title: C++ Reference to a Vector
summary: Shows that vector<int>& v2 = v1 creates an alias for v1. No new vector is created; v2 is just another name for the same vector object.
main_text: Given 'vector<int> v1;', the declaration 'vector<int>& v2 = v1;' creates a C++ Reference. v2 is now an alias (another name) for v1. The memory diagram shows the vector at address 2c0 with its internal structure (data pointer, capacity 10, size 6, underlying array [50,51,52,53,54,10]). Both v1 and v2 labels appear on the same object. A crossed-out icon emphasizes that no new vector is allocated. This is in stark contrast to a pointer (which would create a new variable holding an address) or a value copy (which would duplicate the entire vector).
notes_text: Compare this with slide 3 where vector<int>* vp created a new pointer variable. Here, vector<int>& v2 creates nothing new -- v2 IS v1. No deep copy occurs, no new memory is allocated.

images.description: Memory diagram showing vector at 2c0 with data/cap/size fields and underlying array, labeled as both v1 and v2 with no-new-memory icon

title: Vector Reference Operations - Question
summary: Poses the question of what happens when push_back(42) is called on reference v2 and v1[0] is set to 8, given v2 is an alias for v1.
main_text: Given 'vector<int> v1;' and 'vector<int>& v2 = v1;', the slide asks what happens when 'v2.push_back(42);' and 'v1[0] = 8;' are executed. Since v2 is an alias for v1, both operations affect the same vector. The memory diagram shows the vector at address 2c0 with capacity 10 and size 6 (before the operations), with the underlying array [50,51,52,53,54,10]. Both v1 and v2 labels reference the same object.
notes_text: This slide sets up the question for students to think about before seeing the answer on the next slide. The key insight is that since v2 IS v1, push_back on v2 adds to v1's array, and modifying v1[0] is visible through v2 as well.

images.description: Memory diagram showing vector at 2c0 with both v1 and v2 labels, capacity 10, size 6, array values before modification

title: Vector Reference Operations - Answer
summary: Shows that push_back and index assignment through either v1 or v2 affect the same vector, proving both names refer to the identical object.
main_text: After executing 'v2.push_back(42);' and 'v1[0] = 8;' on a vector where v2 is a reference to v1, both operations happen on the same vector. The updated vector now has size 7 (was 6), with values [8, 51, 52, 53, 54, 10, 42]. The first element changed from 50 to 8 (via v1[0] = 8), and 42 was appended (via v2.push_back(42)). The explanation states: 'Both operations happen on the same vector. v2 is just another name for v1.' This confirms that references provide complete access to the original object.
notes_text: This conclusively demonstrates that references are true aliases. Any operation through either name affects the same underlying object. There is no concept of one name being 'primary' -- both v1 and v2 are equally valid names for the same vector.

images.description: Memory diagram showing updated vector with values [8, 51, 52, 53, 54, 10, 42] after both operations, still labeled as both v1 and v2

title: C++ Reference Syntax Summary - Creates Nothing
summary: Summarizes that declaring T& creates nothing new in memory. It simply associates another name (alias) to an existing variable of type T.
main_text: Given a T variable/object 'T varname;', declaring a T& creates NOTHING. It simply associates another name: 'T& alias = varname;'. This is contrasted with pointer declaration (T*) which creates a new variable that stores an address. The visual uses a suitcase metaphor where the original variable is represented as a suitcase at address 0x2f0, and the alias is represented as a name tag attached directly to the same suitcase, not as a separate entity. The labels 'varname' and 'alias' both point to the same suitcase.
notes_text: The emphasis on 'creates NOTHING' (highlighted) is intentional. Students often mistakenly think int& creates something new like int* does. The suitcase metaphor helps: a pointer is a separate luggage tag, while a reference is just writing another name directly on the suitcase.

images.description: Suitcase metaphor showing a T object at 0x2f0 with both varname and alias as name tags directly on the same suitcase

title: Address-Of vs C++ Reference - Two Meanings of &
summary: Explains that the & operator has two meanings: address-of in expressions (for pointers) and C++ reference/alias in type declarations.
main_text: The & operator is used in TWO contexts and means different things. Students must know how to interpret it in each context. Address-of (for pointers): When & appears in an expression (right side of assignment), it means 'get the address of this variable.' Example: 'int y; int* z = &y;' -- here &y yields the address of y. C++ Reference (Alias): When & appears in a type declaration, it creates a reference. Example: 'int y; int& z = y;' -- here int& declares z as a reference (alias) to y. The side-by-side comparison highlights the visual difference: &y (expression) vs int& z (declaration).
notes_text: This is a critical disambiguation slide. The same character & has completely different meanings depending on context. In a declaration (attached to a type like int&), it means reference. In an expression (prefixed to a variable like &y), it means address-of. Confusing these is a common student error.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison boxes: left box labeled 'Address-of (for pointers)' showing 'int y; int* z = &y;', right box labeled 'C++ Reference (Alias)' showing 'int y; int& z = y;'

title: Address-Of vs C++ Reference - Quick Recognition Guide
summary: Provides a quick recognition rule: & before a variable in an expression means address-of; T& in a declaration means C++ reference/alias.
main_text: Quick rules for recognizing & usage: The & symbol means address-of when used in an expression, written as &variable. It means C++ reference/alias when used in a declaration, written as T& (where T is a type). The left box shows 'Address-of (for pointers)' with the pattern '.. &y ..' indicating & appearing before a variable name in an expression context. The right box shows 'C++ Reference (Alias)' with the pattern 'T& ...' indicating & appearing after a type name in a declaration context. This quick visual guide helps students instantly identify which meaning of & is being used.
notes_text: A practical rule of thumb: if & is next to a type (int&, vector<int>&), it is a reference declaration. If & is next to a variable name in an expression (&y, &myvar), it is the address-of operator.

images.description: Two side-by-side boxes showing the pattern for address-of (&y in expression) and C++ reference (T& in declaration)

title: Why Use C++ References - Pass-By-Reference
summary: Answers why we want aliases: the primary use case is PASS-BY-REFERENCE to FUNCTIONS, enabling functions to modify caller's variables.
main_text: The slide asks: Why would we want to create an alias (C++ Reference)? The answer, displayed prominently: PASS-BY-REFERENCE to FUNCTIONS! This is the primary motivation for C++ references. By passing a reference to a function, the function receives an alias to the caller's variable, allowing it to modify the original variable directly. This avoids the limitations of pass-by-value (where the function only gets a copy) without requiring the explicit pointer syntax that many find confusing.
notes_text: While references can be used for local aliases, 95% of their usage is for function parameters. This motivates the entire concept -- references exist primarily to make pass-by-reference easier and cleaner than using pointers.

title: Recall: Pass-by-Value and the System Stack
summary: Reviews pass-by-value: each function has its own stack memory for locals, arguments, and return link. A copy is made so the original cannot be modified.
main_text: Each function has its own memory on the system stack where all data related to the function is stored, including: local variables, arguments to the function, and return link (where to return to the calling code). By default, parameters are passed-by-value (a copy is made). Thus, one function CANNOT modify the data of another. The alternative is pass-by-reference using pointers. The code example shows: void dec(int); int main() { int y = 3; dec(y); cout << y << endl; // prints 3 } void dec(int y) { y--; }. The stack diagram shows main's y at 0x7bf8 with value 3, and dec's y (a copy) at 0x7bf0 with value 2. Since dec modifies its own copy, main's y remains 3.
notes_text: The stack diagram is essential for understanding why pass-by-value doesn't allow modification. Each function frame is independent -- dec's y is a completely separate variable from main's y, even though they share the same name.

images.description: Stack Area of RAM diagram showing main's frame (y=3 at 0x7bf8, return link at 0x7bfc) and dec's frame (y=2 at 0x7bf0, return link at 0x7bf4), demonstrating separate copies

title: Pass-by-Reference Using Pointers
summary: Shows how pointers enable pass-by-reference by passing addresses. The callee dereferences the pointer to modify the caller's variable directly.
main_text: To allow a function to modify the data of another, we pass pointers. But that syntax is a bit confusing. Is there an easier way? Yes! C++ References. These are likely pointers behind the scenes but simplify the syntax and semantics. The code example shows: int main() { int y = 3; dec(&y); cout << y << endl; // prints 2 } void dec(int* ptr) { *ptr = *ptr - 1; // or (*ptr)--; }. The caller passes &y (address of y), and the callee receives it as int* ptr. To modify y, the callee must dereference with *ptr. The stack diagram shows dec's ptr at 0x7bf0 containing value 7bf8 (main's y address), with the arrow showing *ptr reaching into main's frame to modify y from 3 to 2.
notes_text: This slide establishes the 'problem' that C++ references solve: pointer syntax for pass-by-reference works but requires explicit & at call site and * for dereferencing. C++ references eliminate both of these syntactic burdens.

images.description: Stack diagram showing dec's frame with ptr holding address 7bf8 pointing into main's frame where y changes from 3 to 2 via dereferencing

title: C++ Reference Variables - Motivation and Benefits
summary: Explains that C++ references still use pointers behind the scenes but provide simpler syntax without explicit dereferencing, making pass-by-reference easier.
main_text: So, you want to use pass-by-reference to allow a function to modify data from another, but you don't like pointers and they confuse you? You CAN understand pointers -- keep working at it. And pointers are necessary in several contexts (dynamic allocation, etc.). But you can also use C++ Reference variables in many contexts. C++ reference variables: STILL pass arguments via pointer/address behind the scenes, BUT use a much simpler syntax (i.e. no more de-referencing). We needed you to know what's actually happening behind the scenes. Thus, we taught you pointers. But you can also use the simplified syntax with C++ references.
notes_text: Important nuance: references are NOT a replacement for pointers. Pointers are still needed for dynamic allocation (new/delete), null values, reassignment to different objects, and arrays. References simply offer a cleaner syntax for the common case of pass-by-reference.

title: A New Way to Pass by Reference - Comparison
summary: Side-by-side comparison of pointer vs reference pass-by-reference. Both produce the same output but references have simpler call-site and function-body syntax.
main_text: Behind the scenes the compiler will essentially access the variable with a pointer, but you get to access it like a normal variable without dereferencing. Think of a reference variable as an alias. OLD WAY (Using pointers): int main() { int y = 3; doit(&y); cout << y << endl; } void doit(int *x) { *x = *x - 1; }. NEW WAY (Using C++ References): int main() { int y = 3; doit(y); cout << y << endl; } void doit(int &x) { x = x - 1; // Ref. declaration }. Output is '2' in both programs. Three memory diagrams show: With Pointers (x stores address 0x1a0), With References Physically (x stores 0x1a0 behind scenes), With References Logically (y and x share the same box with value 3).
notes_text: The three-way memory comparison is key. Physically, references work like pointers (storing addresses). Logically, you should think of them as aliases (same box, two names). The caller syntax is cleaner too: doit(y) instead of doit(&y).

images.description: Three memory diagrams comparing pointer approach (separate box for x holding address), reference physical view (similar to pointer), and reference logical view (shared box with both y and x names)

title: Correct Usage of Pointers - Multiply Example
summary: Shows correct pointer usage with a multiply function that uses an output pointer parameter. Demonstrates how pointers let functions write results to caller variables.
main_text: Commonly functions will take some inputs and produce some outputs. This example uses a simple 'multiply' function to practice with pointers. Two versions are shown: int mul1(int in1, int in2) returns the product directly, while void mul2(int in1, int in2, int* out) writes the result through a pointer. The main function: int wid = 8, len = 5, a; mul2(wid, len, &a); cout << "Ans. is " << a << endl;. The stack diagram shows mul's frame with in1=8, in2=5, out=0xbf8 (pointing to main's a). After execution, main's a is updated from uninitialized (-732) to 40. The function mul2 computes *out = in1 * in2.
notes_text: This sets up the comparison with the reference version on the next slide. Note how the pointer version requires &a at the call site and *out for dereferencing in the function body. The reference version will eliminate both of these.

images.description: Stack diagram showing mul's frame (in1=8, in2=5, out=0xbf8) and main's frame (wid=8, len=5, a changing from -732 to 40), with out pointing to a

title: Multiply Example with C++ References
summary: Shows the same multiply function using C++ reference parameter int& out instead of int* out. Simpler syntax at both call site and function body.
main_text: We can pass using C++ reference. The reference 'out' is just an alias for 'a' back in main. In memory, it might actually be a pointer, but you don't have to dereference. The code: void mul(int in1, int in2, int& out); int main() { int wid = 8, len = 5, a; mul(wid, len, a); cout << "Ans. is " << a << endl; }. void mul(int in1, int in2, int& out) { out = in1 * in2; }. Note: the call is mul(wid, len, a) not mul(wid, len, &a), and the function body uses out = in1 * in2 not *out = in1 * in2. The stack diagram shows mul's frame with out labeled '?0xbf8?' indicating it may hold a pointer behind the scenes, but logically 'out' is an alias for main's 'a'.
notes_text: Compare with slide 19: the call site drops the & operator, and the function body drops the * operator. The result is identical -- a gets the value 40. This demonstrates the syntactic advantage of references over pointers for output parameters.

images.description: Stack diagram showing mul's frame with in1=8, in2=5, out (possibly holding address behind scenes) aliasing main's a, with a updated to 40

title: Swap with Pointers - Pass-by-Reference Example
summary: Classic swap function using pointers. Addresses of x and y are passed, and dereferencing is used to swap values at those addresses.
main_text: Classic example of issues with local variables: writing a function to swap two variables. Pass-by-reference using pointers does work. Addresses of the actual x,y variables in main are passed, and those addresses are used to change the physical memory locations. Code: void swap2(int* x, int* y); int main() { int x=5, y=7; swap2(&x, &y); cout << " x=" << x; cout << " y=" << y << endl; }. void swap2(int* px, int* py) { int temp = *px; *px = *py; *py = temp; }. The stack diagram shows swap2's frame with temp=5, px=0x7bf0 (pointing to main's x), py=0x7bf4 (pointing to main's y). After swap, main's x becomes 7 and y becomes 5.
notes_text: The swap function is a classic example because it requires modifying two caller variables. Return values can only return one thing, so pass-by-reference (via pointers or references) is necessary. Note the complexity: &x, &y at call; *px, *py for access.

images.description: Stack diagram showing swap2's frame with temp, px pointing to main's x, py pointing to main's y, with values being swapped from 5,7 to 7,5

title: Swap with C++ References - Cleaner Syntax
summary: Same swap function using C++ references instead of pointers. Syntax is much cleaner: no & at call site, no * for dereferencing in function body.
main_text: Pass-by-reference with C++ References makes the syntax cleaner. Behind scenes it is likely still passing pointers. Code: void swap2(int& rx, int& ry); int main() { int x=5, y=7; swap2(x, y); cout << " x=" << x; cout << " y=" << y << endl; }. void swap2(int& rx, int& ry) { int temp = rx; rx = ry; ry = temp; }. The call site uses swap2(x, y) instead of swap2(&x, &y). The function body uses rx and ry directly instead of *px and *py. The stack diagram shows swap2's frame with temp=5, and rx/ry shown as aliases (dashed boxes) pointing to main's x and y. After swap, x=7 and y=5.
notes_text: Comparing with slide 21, the reference version is significantly simpler: the call looks like a normal function call swap2(x,y), and the function body looks like it is working with normal variables. The dashed boxes for rx and ry in the stack indicate they may hold addresses behind the scenes.

images.description: Stack diagram showing swap2's frame with temp=5, rx and ry as dashed alias boxes pointing to main's x and y, with values swapped to 7 and 5

title: Vector Arguments - Pass-by-Value Question
summary: Poses the question: when do_it() takes a vector by value and pushes back 60, what will the original myvec contain after the call?
main_text: The code creates a vector myvec with values [50, 51, 52, 53, 54] (size 5, capacity 5). The function do_it takes a vector<int> by value: void do_it(vector<int> v) { v.push_back(60); }. When do_it(myvec) is called, the question asks what the contents of myvec will be after do_it returns. Since the parameter is passed by value, do_it receives a copy of myvec. The diagram shows myvec at address 240 with data pointer, capacity 5, and size 5.
notes_text: This sets up the key lesson about vectors and pass-by-value. Students should predict that myvec remains unchanged because do_it only modifies its local copy. The next slide confirms this.

images.description: Memory diagram of myvec showing data pointer at 240, capacity 5, size 5, with underlying array [50, 51, 52, 53, 54]

title: Vector Pass-By-Value - Deep Copy Behavior
summary: Demonstrates that vector pass-by-value creates a deep copy. Modifications to the copy in do_it do not affect the original myvec in main.
main_text: The vector class makes a deep copy when passing-by-value. If we want to modify the vector in another function, we'd have to pass by reference. When do_it(myvec) is called with void do_it(vector<int> v), a complete deep copy is created: v gets its own data pointer (at address 760), its own capacity (10), size (6 after push_back), and its own copy of the array [50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 60]. The comment in the code says: 'v.push_back(60); // only adds to v (the copy) // not myvec'. The original myvec remains unchanged with its original 5 elements. Two separate memory diagrams show myvec (unchanged) and v (with 60 appended).
notes_text: Deep copy means all the underlying data is duplicated, not just the vector metadata. This is expensive for large vectors -- both in time (copying all elements) and memory (doubling storage). This motivates pass-by-reference for large objects.

images.description: Two separate vector diagrams: myvec (unchanged, 5 elements at 240) and v (copy with 6 elements at 760 including the appended 60)

title: Vector Pass-By-Reference - Pointer vs Reference Comparison
summary: Compares two approaches to pass a vector by reference: using vector<int>* (pointer) vs vector<int>& (reference). Both modify the original vector.
main_text: Which do you prefer? Even if we didn't want to modify the vector but just look at the data, why might we want to pass by reference? (Answer: to avoid expensive deep copies.) Two side-by-side code examples show: Pointer version: void do_it(vector<int>* v1) { v1->push_back(60); } called with do_it(&myvec);. Reference version: void do_it(vector<int>& v2) { v2.push_back(60); } called with do_it(myvec);. Both modify the original myvec. The memory diagram shows myvec at 2e0 with v2 as an alias, after push_back(60) the vector has 6 elements [50,51,52,53,54,60]. The pointer version uses v1->push_back and &myvec; the reference version uses v2.push_back and just myvec.
notes_text: This slide highlights two key reasons for pass-by-reference: (1) to modify the original, and (2) to avoid expensive copies even when not modifying. The reference syntax is clearly simpler -- dot notation instead of arrow, no & at call site.

images.description: Memory diagram showing myvec at 2e0 with v2 as alias (dashed), vector containing [50,51,52,53,54,60] after push_back

title: When to Use References - Reason 1: Modify Caller Data
summary: First reason to use references: when you want to actually modify an input parameter of the calling function, such as modifying a GradeBook object.
main_text: Reason 1: Whenever you want to actually modify an input parameter/argument of the calling function (e.g. modify a local variable from another function). Example shows a GradeBook class with a large 2D array: class GradeBook { public: int grades[8][100]; // Large amount of data };. In main: GradeBook gb; double average = process_it(gb);. The function change_it(GradeBook& mygb) takes the GradeBook by reference, allowing it to modify the original: mygb.grades[0][0] = 91;. The diagram shows gb as a large object in main, with mygb being an alias that directly references gb.
notes_text: The GradeBook example is chosen because it contains 800 ints (8x100 array = 3200 bytes), making deep copies expensive. Passing by reference both avoids the copy and allows modification. The 'Editor' label on mygb indicates it has write access.

images.description: Diagram showing gb object in main as a grid, with mygb as a reference alias pointing to gb, labeled 'Editor' indicating write access

title: When to Use References - Reason 2: Avoid Copies
summary: Second reason: to avoid making a copy when passing big struct or class objects. No copy is made, saving time, even when only reading data.
main_text: Reason 1: Whenever you want to actually modify an input parameter/argument of the calling function. Reason 2: To avoid making a copy when passing big struct or class objects. Because no copy will be made, pass-by-value would have wasted time copying contents to new memory. The code example shows double average_it(GradeBook& mygb) which only reads data (summing all grades) without modifying gb: double sum = 0; for(int i=0; i<8; i++) for(int j=0; j<100; j++) sum += mygb.grades[i][j]; sum /= (8*100); return sum;. Even though average_it only reads, passing by reference avoids copying the entire 800-element array.
notes_text: This reveals an important design consideration: even read-only functions benefit from pass-by-reference for large objects. However, this opens the door to accidental modification, which motivates const references on the next slide.

images.description: Diagram showing gb in main with mygb as reference alias pointing to gb, used for read-only averaging computation

title: When to Use References - Caution: Accidental Modification
summary: Warns that passing by reference opens the door to accidental modification. Asks whether there is a way to get speed without risking changes.
main_text: Reason 1: Modify input parameters. Reason 2: Avoid making copies for large objects. Caution: But by passing a reference, we open the door to modification. Is there a way we can NOT make a copy (speed) but prevent modification (protection)? YES!! The code example shows average_it(GradeBook& mygb) which is supposed to only compute an average, but accidentally includes mygb.grades[0][0] = 91; -- an unintended modification that corrupts the original data. Since mygb is a non-const reference, the compiler allows this modification silently. This motivates the need for const references.
notes_text: This slide creates the 'aha moment' for students: references give both speed and write access, but sometimes we only want speed without write access. The accidental modification example (grades[0][0] = 91 in a function meant to only compute an average) is realistic and motivating.

images.description: Diagram showing gb in main with mygb reference, code highlighting accidental modification mygb.grades[0][0] = 91

title: Const References - Speed with Protection
summary: Introduces const references: no copy is made (fast), and the compiler prevents modification (safe). Provides both performance and data protection.
main_text: Solution: const references. Fast: NO COPY made! Just an alias. Protection: Compiler will double check for modification and generate an error. Remember you are your own worst enemy. The compiler will produce an error to tell you that you have written code that will modify the object you said should be constant. It doesn't protect against back-doors like pointers that somehow point at these data objects (compiler check only). The code example: double average_it(const GradeBook& mygb). The function can read mygb.grades[i][j] normally, but the line mygb.grades[0][0] = 91; will cause a compiler error. The mygb reference is labeled 'Viewer' instead of 'Editor', indicating read-only access.
notes_text: The const keyword applied to a reference gives the best of both worlds: no copy overhead (like a regular reference) plus compile-time protection against modification (like pass-by-value). This is the recommended default for passing large objects to functions that only read them.

images.description: Diagram showing gb in main with mygb as const reference alias labeled 'Viewer' indicating read-only access, with compiler error on modification attempt

title: Large Object Suggestions - Pass-by-Value vs Const Reference
summary: Recommends using const reference for large objects like vectors and strings to get copy safety with pass-by-value's protection against modification.
main_text: When you pass a large object (e.g. vector, deque, or even a C++ string) to a function, a copy will be made. SLOW!! The advantage of a copy is that the function CANNOT alter the original object (e.g. vector, Quad, etc.). But passing by const reference saves time and provides the same security. Code example: void do_something1(vector<int> v) -- pass-by-value with lock icon (safe but slow, makes a copy). void do_something2(const vector<int>& v) -- const reference with 'Viewer' label (safe AND fast, no copy). The question asks: can myvec be different upon return from each? For do_something1 (by value), myvec cannot change. For do_something2 (const ref), myvec also cannot change -- but no copy was made.
notes_text: This is the practical recommendation students should follow: for any large object parameter where the function only reads data, use const T& (const reference). This applies to vectors, strings, maps, sets, custom classes, and any other large objects.

title: Pass by Reference - Vector Sum Example with Stack Diagram
summary: Shows a complete example of passing a vector by const reference to a sum function. Stack diagram shows no copy of the vector data is made.
main_text: Notice no copy of x needs to be made since we pass it to sum() by reference. Notice that likely the computer passes the address to sum() but you should just think of dat as an alias for x. The const keyword tells the compiler to double check that we don't modify the vector (giving the safety of pass-by-value but the performance of pass-by-reference). Code: int sum(const vector<int>&); int main() { int result; vector<int> x(100); // fill x with {98, 95, 87, 92, ...}; result = sum(x); }. int sum(const vector<int>& dat) { int s = 0; for(size_t i=0; i < dat.size(); i++) { s += dat[i]; } return s; }. Stack diagram shows sum's frame with s=0 and dat (holding address 0xbf0 behind scenes), while main's x has ptr=0x55080 and len=100 with the actual data array at 0x550080.
notes_text: The stack diagram reveals the implementation: dat in sum's frame likely holds the address of x (0xbf0), but logically dat IS x. The '= dat' annotation on main's frame shows the alias relationship. Using size_t for the loop variable is good practice with .size().

images.description: Stack diagram showing sum's frame (s=0, dat pointing to main's x) and main's frame (x with ptr/len, result), with actual data array at 0x550080

title: More Details of C++ References - Rules and Restrictions
summary: Covers detailed rules: references are not variables, must be assigned at declaration, cannot be reassigned, and are primarily used for function parameters.
main_text: 95% of the usage of reference type (T&) is for passing arguments to a function by reference. However, we can create aliases within the same local function. Rules: T& is NOT another variable; does NOT require memory (e.g. int& doesn't store an int, but is an alias for an actual int variable). MUST assign to the reference variable when you declare it (an alias doesn't exist on its own, but must be tied to a real variable). Unlike pointers, what actual variable is referenced cannot be changed (once we create a reference to a variable, it cannot refer to any other). Code example: int main() { int y; int &x = y; // x is NOT another variable, it's an alias. x = 3; // Sets y to 3. x++; // increment y. cout << y << endl; // 4 prints. int &z; // NO! must assign. int w = 5; x = w; // doesn't make x reference w... copies w into y. return 0; }
notes_text: Three critical rules: (1) Must initialize at declaration -- int &z; alone is illegal. (2) Cannot be reassigned -- x = w copies w's value into y, it does not make x an alias for w. (3) References don't occupy memory logically. The physical vs logical memory diagrams reinforce this.

images.description: Two memory diagrams: physical view showing y at 0x1a0 with value 3 and x holding address 0x1a0, logical view showing y and x sharing the same box with value 3

title: Pointers vs References Summary Table
summary: Summary table showing how & and * behave differently in type declarations versus expressions. Key reference for distinguishing pointers and references.
main_text: How to tell references and pointers apart: Check if you see the '&' or '*' in a type declaration or expression. The table has two columns: 'With a Type' and 'In an Expression'. For &: With a Type -- indicates a C++ Reference Var (int &val, vector<int> &vec). In an Expression -- Address-of yields a pointer to the object, adds a * to the type of variable (int x; int* p; p = &x;). For *: With a Type -- Declares a pointer type variable (int *valptr = &val, vector<int> *vecptr = &vec). In an Expression -- De-Reference (Value @ address), cancels a * from the type of variable (int* p = new int; *p = 5;).
notes_text: This table is a critical reference that students should memorize. The dual meaning of both & and * depending on context (declaration vs expression) is one of the most common sources of confusion in C++. 'With a type' = declaration context; 'In an expression' = usage context.

images.description: 2x2 table comparing & and * behavior in type declarations versus expressions, with code examples for each cell

title: Backup Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide marking the beginning of backup/supplementary material for additional reference on C++ references and pointers.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the BACKUP section, which contains supplementary material for additional reference and review.
notes_text: Backup slides provide additional examples and summaries for students who want more practice or a different perspective on the material.

title: Kinds of References - Pointers vs C++ Reference Variables
summary: Side-by-side comparison of pointers and C++ reference variables. Pointers are variables that store addresses; references are aliases that occupy no memory.
main_text: Pointers: A variable (like any other) which occupies memory and stores an address of another variable and can be updated (like any other variable) to store a new address to some other variable. Declared with the T* syntax (e.g. int*, char*, Item*). C++ Reference Variable: A special declaration that simply gives a second (or third, or fourth) name to an already-declared variable. Declared with the T& syntax (e.g. int&, string&, Item&). Does not occupy any memory (just tells the compiler to allow another name to reference some other variable). Important Note: When we use the general term 'reference' as in 'pass-by-reference' we can use EITHER pointers OR C++ Reference Variables.
notes_text: Key distinctions: Pointers occupy memory, can be null, can be reassigned, and require dereferencing. References occupy no memory (logically), cannot be null, cannot be reassigned, and use normal variable syntax. Both can achieve pass-by-reference.

title: Swap Two Variables Summary - Three Approaches
summary: Compares three swap implementations: pass-by-value (fails), pass-by-pointer (works), and pass-by-C++ reference (works). Shows output for each.
main_text: Pass-by-value passes a copy. Pass-by-reference has two sub-approaches: Pass-by-pointer/address passes address of actual variable. Pass-by-C++-reference passes an alias to actual variable. Three side-by-side code examples: (1) Pass-by-value: void swapit(int x, int y) { int temp; temp = x; x = y; y = temp; } -- Output: x=5,y=7 (swap fails, only copies were swapped). (2) Pass-by-pointer: void swapit(int *px, int *py) { int temp; temp = *px; *px = *py; *py = temp; } called with swapit(&x,&y) -- Output: x=7,y=5 (swap works). (3) Pass-by-C++-reference: void swapit(int &rx, int &ry) { int temp; temp = rx; rx = ry; ry = temp; } called with swapit(x,y) -- Output: x=7,y=5 (swap works).
notes_text: This summary slide is excellent for exam review. The three versions side-by-side make the differences crystal clear: value fails, pointer works but is verbose, reference works and is clean. Both reference approaches produce the same result.

title: Misuse of Pointers and References - Dangling References
summary: Warns against returning a pointer or reference to a local variable. When the function returns, the local variable is destroyed, leaving a dangling pointer/reference.
main_text: Make sure you don't return a pointer or reference to a dead variable. You might get lucky and find that old value still there, but likely you won't. Code example: int* badmul1(int in1, int in2) { int out = in1 * in2; return &out; } -- BAD! Returns a pointer to a var that will go out of scope. int& badmul2(int in1, int in2) { int out = in1 * in2; return out; } -- BAD! Returns a reference to a var that will go out of scope. In main: int *a = badmul1(wid,len); cout << *a << endl; -- the value at the address may have been overwritten. The stack diagram shows badmul1's frame with out=40 at 0xbe0, and main's a storing 0xbe0. After badmul1 returns, the memory at 0xbe0 is reclaimed and may contain garbage.
notes_text: This is a critical safety lesson. Local variables live on the stack and are destroyed when their function returns. Returning a pointer or reference to them creates undefined behavior. The correct approach is to return by value (return in1*in2;) or use dynamic allocation.

images.description: Stack diagram showing badmul1's frame (out=40 at 0xbe0) and main's frame (a storing 0xbe0), illustrating that after badmul1 returns, the memory at 0xbe0 is invalid

title: Using C++ References - Pointer and Reference Equivalence
summary: Shows that a pointer provides a second way to reference a variable. *ptr and y can be used interchangeably when ptr points to y.
main_text: A pointer is like a 2nd way to reference some other variable (e.g. y). We can use *ptr and y interchangeably. Code example: int main() { int y; int *ptr = &y; // address-of operator. *ptr = 3; // Sets y to 3. y = 3; // Same as above. }. The 'With Pointers' memory diagram shows y at address 0x1a0 holding value 3, with ptr below it holding the address 0x1a0 and an arrow pointing up to y. This reinforces that dereferencing a pointer (*ptr) accesses the same memory as using the variable name directly.
notes_text: This backup slide reinforces the fundamental pointer concept: *ptr is equivalent to y when ptr holds &y. This equivalence is analogous to how a reference z would also be equivalent to y if declared as int& z = y, but without needing the * syntax.

images.description: Memory diagram showing y at 0x1a0 with value 3, and ptr below holding 0x1a0 with arrow pointing to y
